The dog was the color of slushy snow, it was mottily grey and shaggy like a pure Irish wolfhound with nothing else in him.
His body was still small, but his paws were as big as bear claws, and we all knew what that meant.
Selma still stood tall in front of the kitchen bench.
She looked at the dog for a long time.
Then she glanced at my father as if he were a gift idea shop.

He was sure that Death would not snatch away his life, but gently take it from his hand.
He imagined how Death would knock cautiously, opening the door just a crack and asking, "May I?", to which Farmer Häubel would naturally respond affirmatively.
"Of course," Farmer Häubel would say, "do come in," and Death would enter.
He'd stand by Farmer Häubel's bed and ask: "Is now a good time?

The people in the village were unsettled; you could tell, even though they mostly tried to conceal it.

This morning, just a few hours after Selma's dream, people in the village moved as if black ice had formed on all paths, not just outside but inside homes as well—black ice in kitchens and living rooms.
They moved as if their own bodies were completely foreign to them; as if all their joints were swollen and also the objects they handled highly flammable.
All day long, they regarded their lives with suspicion and others' lives too where possible.

They constantly glanced behind them to check if someone possessed with murderous intent might be running up—an individual who'd lost his mind and therefore had nothing notable left to lose—and quickly looked back ahead because such individuals could certainly attack from the front too.
They looked upwards to rule out any roof tiles or heavy lampshades falling down onto them.
They avoided all animals because, they believed things could break free from animals faster than humans.
They steered clear of benign cows—which might kick today—they avoided dogs (even old ones that could hardly stand), which perhaps may savage their throats today anyway.
Except for Selma's sister-in-law Elsbeth, the people in the village were mostly not superstitious.

They casually did all those things that are taboo when it comes to superstition: they sat quietly under wall clocks, even though superstitions predict dying from it; they slept with their heads facing the door, even though according to superstition this means that you'll soon be carried out feet first through that very door.
They hung laundry between Christmas and New Year's Eve which, as Elsbeth warned, according to superstition is tantamount to suicide or assisting in a murder.
They weren't scared when the owl called at night, when a horse in the barn was sweating heavily or when a dog howled at night with its head down.
The train ride lasted fifteen minutes, with no stops in between.
Since our first train ride, we'd always play the same game:
We'd stand with our backs to the windows near the opposite train doors.
Martin closed his eyes while I looked out of the door's window right behind Martin.
In first grade, I described everything I saw during our journey to Martin who would try to memorize it all.

He succeeded so well that by second grade I wouldn't have to list anything anymore and he could recite almost everything that I was seeing out of the foggy train window while standing with his back towards it and closing his eyes: "Wire factory," he said right as we were passing it by; "Now a field.

She had started up after the image of the okapi withdrew; sitting upright in bed she had awakened and stared at her nightgown—in which she was supposedly standing on Uhlheck in her dream—and then at the clock.
.. three o'clock.
"We probably shouldn't take this too seriously," advised Selma with all seriousness as if she were a TV detective trying to downplay an anonymous threatening letter.
"What's the matter?", I asked.
"Nothing," Selma trilled, opened the refrigerator, pulled out a pack of sliced cheese and some liverwurst and waved them through the air.
"What would you like on your sandwich today? she trilled.
"Little mouse," she added in that same singsong voice, and now her tune and little mouse' formed an alarming combination.
"Cheese, please," I said, "what's wrong with you?"  "Nothing," Selma trilled again, "I told you".
She then spread butter on a slice of bread; still flopping about loosely, her wrist inadvertently brushed against the cheese which got knocked off from the countertop.
Now motionless, Selma stared down at the packet of cheese as if it were some precious thing that had shattered into a thousand pieces.
Selma had dreamt of an Okapi three times in her life, and each time someone had died afterwards; therefore, we were convinced that dreaming of an Okapi and death were invariably linked.
Our minds work like that.
They can rapidly associate the most unrelated things as being intrinsically connected.
Like coffee pots and shoelaces, or deposit bottles and fir trees for instance.
When I slept downstairs with Selma, she would tell me bedtime stories with happy endings.
When I was smaller, I always held her wrist after the stories, putting my thumb on her pulse and imagining that the whole world did everything to the rhythm of Selma's heartbeat.

I imagined how the optician ground his lenses, Martin lifted a weight, Elsbeth trimmed her hedge; how the retailer arranged juice boxes; my mother layered pine twigs; my father stamped prescriptions; and they all did it exactly in time with Selma's heart rhythm.
That reliably sent me to sleep every time, but now at ten years old, Selma decided that I was too old for that.
